title: Unlocking the therapeutic potential of immuno-radiotherapy: insights from preclinical and clinical research

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Unlocking the therapeutic potential of immuno-radiotherapy: insights from preclinical and clinical research》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · s0001-p1】Cancer cells can evade immune responses,1 causing a need for therapies that potentiate antitumor immunity, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). These antibodies restore the antitumor immune activity by blocking inhibitory interactions between cancer cells or antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and immune cells.2 ICIs targeting cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) and programmed cell death (ligand) 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) have become central to cancer treatment.3-6 However, durable responses remain limited due to tumor resistance.7 To improve outcomes, combination strategies with other immunostimulatory treatments are employed, including radiotherapy (RT).8 RT, historically regarded as a local treatment, is now recognized for its systemic immunomodulatory properties. These effects range from immunosuppression—such as lymphopenia,9-12 TGF-β-mediated promotion of anti-inflammatory immune cells,13,14 and increased expression of immune checkpoint molecules—to immunostimulation via induction of immunogenic cell death (ICD), activation of the cyclic GMP–AMP (cGAMP) synthase (cGAS)/stimulator of interferon (IFN) genes (STING) pathway and type I IFN signaling, reshaping of the cellular and cytokine/chemokine environment, and vasculature remodeling.15-18 The abscopal effect, defined as a regression of tumors outside the irradiation field, is a compelling example of RT-induced immunomodulation, though historically rare.19 The recent implementation of ICI in the clinic for patients receiving RT has significantly increased the occurrence of abscopal responses.20-24 This highlights the synergistic potential between RT and ICI, as RT can enhance tumor antigen presentation and immune infiltration, thereby priming the immune system for a more effective response to ICI. RT's immunomodulatory potential, broad accessibility25 and distinct toxicity profile relative to immunotherapy26-28 further support their combination. Together, these complementary modalities have led to the emergence of immuno-RT (iRT), a promising therapeutic approach that leverages the strengths of both treatments to improve patient outcomes. In this review, we highlight recent preclinical and clinical applications of iRT and discuss factors influencing its efficacy to optimize the design of future studies and trials.

【Preclinical evidence of iRT-mediated systemic immune activation · s0002-s2001-p1】Several immunotherapies have been investigated in combination with RT across various preclinical in vivo models, showing superior efficacy of iRT over monotherapies and reporting abscopal effects (Table 1). Besides RT combination with ICIs, other immunotherapies have been investigated, including adoptive cell therapy (ACT), vaccination, cytokines, chemokines and immunocytokines, and viruses. The benefits of these combinations surpass local tumor control and can yield systemic immune activation and abscopal effects, establish long-lasting immune memory protective against tumor rechallenge, known as “in situ vaccination”, induce complete responses (CRs) and extend survival.29 These preclinical studies enable the investigation of a wide range of experimental conditions that would be unfeasible in clinical settings. This allows the dissection of the mechanisms underlying iRT by identifying cellular mediators of the abscopal effect, such as CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, dendritic cells (DCs), and macrophages, thereby revealing novel immune targets beyond immune checkpoints. Yet, clinical translation remains challenging, partly due to animal model constraints, such as the limited diversity and relevance of available murine tumor models.

sections.text:

【Roadmap for preclinical investigation of iRT abscopal effect · s0002-s2002-p2】While most iRT studies use immunocompetent or partially immunodeficient syngeneic mice, more advanced models have emerged. Humanized mice engrafted with a human immune system allow the in vivo study of human tumor–immune interactions. Unlike immunocompetent models, they support longer-term studies, owing to a slower tumor growth, and can be used with both cell-derived xenografts (CDXs) and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs).71-73 While most studies are conducted in allograft settings, PDX autograft models offer a path toward personalized medicine.74 In these models, mice are engrafted with a patient's immune system and matched tumor creating “clone mice” to his image.75-77 Yet humanized mice present limitations beyond their high cost and time-consuming nature, including incomplete immune reconstitution, lack of lymph nodes impairing T cell priming, allogeneic non-antigen-specific immune responses, and limited interactions between murine host cells and the human immune system or human tumor.74,77

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Unlocking the therapeutic potential of immuno-radiotherapy: insights from preclinical and clinical research》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusions · s0005-p1】Growing preclinical and clinical evidence supports the synergy between immunotherapy and RT, yielding local and systemic benefits, including durable antitumor immunity and abscopal responses. However, the clinical benefits remain modest compared to preclinical findings. Bridging this gap requires next-generation preclinical models and a deeper understanding of the biological mechanisms driving iRT efficacy. Emerging modulators, such as the gut microbiome and tumor aneuploidy, add further complexity to iRT optimization.

【Conclusions · s0005-p2】Key research priorities fall into three main axes (Figure 2): (A) optimizing treatment delivery: RT regimen, sequence with ICI, field and type of RT; (B) optimizing irradiated tissue parameters: normal tissue effect, and choice of irradiated lesion; and (C) optimizing patient selection through biomarker identification. Addressing these priorities will ultimately help resolve two major questions in the field: how can RT be harnessed to stimulate the immune system while avoiding immune suppression, and what are reliable markers of iRT response?

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《Unlocking the therapeutic potential of immuno-radiotherapy: insights from preclinical and clinical research》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · f0001】Figure 1. Roadmap for preclinical in vivo iRT studies: investigating the antitumor effects of immuno-radiotherapy require optimal study design. (1) Selection of a mouse model: immunocompetent, immunodeficient, or humanized. (2) Selection of a tumor model: genetically- or carcinogen-induced; cell-derived xenografts, which can be engrafted subcutaneously, intravenously, or orthotopically; or patient-derived xenografts. (3) Treatment selection based on clinical guidelines or preclinical studies for the appropriate dose and duration (immunotherapy) and characterization of cancer cell radiosensitivity by colony formation assay. (4) Monitoring of treatment effects macroscopically, reporting tumor growth and mouse survival. And microscopically reporting targets such as immunogenic cell death markers (DAMPs), cGAS/STING pathway activation and immune cells in the blood, tumors and lymphoid organs. Timing must be cautiously considered for microscopic monitoring. (5) Confirm observations of antitumor immunity by performing immune-depleting experiments using partially immunodeficient mice or depleting antibodies; performing rechallenge experiments with cancer cells; or ex vivo characterization of immune cell activity. GEMM: genetically engineered mouse model; CDX: cell-derived xenograft; PDX: patient-derived xenograft; DAMP: damage-associated molecular pattern; cGAS/STING: cyclic GMP–AMP synthase/stimulator of interferon genes; and Ab: antibody.

【Figure 2. · f0002】Figure 2. Updated determining factors for optimal immuno-radiotherapy: optimal combinations of immuno-radiotherapy (iRT) rely on seven key factors, categorized into three axes: (A) treatment delivery: (1) dose-fractionation regimens of radiotherapy (RT) that promote antitumor immunity, spare circulating peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), induce vascular remodeling while preventing the activation of immunosuppressive pathways, i.e. through three prime repair exonuclease 1 (TREX1) upregulation; (2) sequence and timing of RT and immunotherapy (IO), which may depend on the immunotherapeutic agent; (3) the radiation field that spares blood vessels and lymphoid organs, or the partial irradiation of the tumor with low-dose RT (LDRT) and with high-dose RT (HDRT) on another tumor region; (4) type of ionizing radiation and their characteristics, such as dose-rate or beam energy. (B) Irradiated tissue parameters: (5) RT effects on normal tissue, including toxicity and benefits depending on the tissue; (6) choice of the lesion to irradiate, considering lesion immunotypes, clonality, and host organs, and the possibility to irradiate multiple lesions. (C) Patient selection: (7) identification of biomarkers predictive of iRT response.

【Figure 3. · f0003】Figure 3. Effects of the dose–fractionation of radiotherapy on the tumor microenvironment: radiotherapy-mediated immunomodulation depends on the regimen used, with doses per fraction varying between LDRT, CFRT, MD-SBRT and HD-SBRT. All of which can induce proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory effects by recruiting or polarizing immune cells in the tumor or by regulating signaling pathways. CFRT is particularly efficient to normalize tumor vasculature, decreasing hypoxia and facilitating immune cell recruitment. MD-SBRT is the preferred range to induce ICD with the release of DAMPs, TAAs, cytokines, chemokines, and activation of the cGAS/STING pathway. Although it induces ICD, HD-SBRT disrupts the vasculature and induces endothelial cell death. Above a certain threshold, HD-SBRT activates TREX1, which impairs type I IFN signaling. RT: radiotherapy; LDRT: low-dose radiotherapy; CFRT: conventional fractionated radiotherapy; MD-SBRT: moderate-dose stereotactic body radiotherapy; HD-SBRT: high-dose stereotactic body radiotherapy; fct: fraction; Th: T helper; Treg: T regulatory; NK: natural killer; DC: dendritic cell; IFN: interferon; IL: interleukin; TGF: transforming growth factor; HIF: hypoxia inducible factor; Arg: arginase; TAA: tumor-associated antigen; ICD: immunogenic cell death; DAMPs: damage-associated molecular patterns; cGAS/STING: cyclic GMP‒AMP synthase/stimulator of interferon genes; TNF: tumor necrosis factor; and TREX1: three prime repair exonuclease 1.
